title: From Trinidad Doubles to Oxtail Bunny Chow: How Drāvida Is Bringing the Full Diaspora to New York's Table
excerpt: Chef Aarthi Sampath's East Village debut maps the global journey of South Asian flavours — and gives NRIs a mirror they rarely see in American restaurants.
body:
The most exciting new Indian restaurant in New York does not serve butter chicken.

At Drāvida, which opened this month in Manhattan's East Village, the marquee dishes include Trinidad-style doubles, South African oxtail bunny chow, Indonesian-inflected idli with shrimp, and Indo-Malay nasi kandar. Together, they trace a culinary map of the South Asian diaspora — the millions who carried their spices, techniques, and food memories from the subcontinent to the Caribbean, East Africa, Southeast Asia, and beyond.

## A Chef's 13-Year New York Education

Chef Aarthi Sampath first wrote the concept for Drāvida in 2019, but the restaurant is the product of a career that spans over a decade in some of New York's most demanding kitchens. After moving from Mumbai in 2013, Sampath trained at Junoon, The Breslin, and the Rainbow Room before gaining national recognition with wins on Food Network's *Chopped* and *Beat Bobby Flay*. She currently sells approximately 50,000 meals weekly through CookUnity.

"This restaurant is for New Yorkers who haven't seen their food represented — for the communities that built this city and whose cuisines haven't always had a place at the table," Sampath said at the opening.

## Beyond the Curry House

Drāvida occupies two floors in a restored 100-year-old building, including original brick ovens. A 20-seat downstairs speakeasy called Jam and Jaggery offers cocktails and small plates. The menu deliberately bypasses the tikka-masala-and-naan playbook that has defined Indian restaurants in America for decades, instead showcasing regional sub-cuisines and the culinary impact of South Asian migration.

The restaurant arrives at a moment when the entire genre is being rewritten. London's Dishoom is on deck for New York later this year in a deal that valued the chain at nearly $400 million. Farzi Café, the Michelin Guide-recognized bistro from restaurateur Zorawar Kalra, just opened its first American location in Bellevue, Washington, with plans to expand coast to coast. And Badmaash, the Los Angeles concept that serves Parle-G ice cream sandwiches and Punjabi-spiced steak frites, opened its third location in Venice Beach.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, Drāvida's menu reads like a family tree. The Trinidad doubles evoke the Chaguanas market and the Indo-Caribbean communities whose ancestors left Bihar and eastern UP as indentured labourers. The bunny chow nods to Durban's Indian population, the largest outside of India. The nasi kandar connects to Malaysia's Mamak stalls.

These are stories that first-generation immigrants carry but rarely see reflected on American menus. Sampath's achievement is not just culinary — it is cartographic, mapping a diaspora that spans continents and centuries onto a single restaurant menu in the East Village.

## What's Next

Drāvida is now accepting reservations through its website. For NRIs visiting New York this summer, it joins a rapidly expanding constellation of progressive Indian restaurants that are making the city the undisputed capital of modern Indian dining in America. The question is no longer whether Indian cuisine can be taken seriously in the United States. It is how many different versions of "Indian" the country is finally ready to embrace.
author: Diaspora Desk
